pages.title: HTTP/1.1 Explained: RFC 9110 and RFC 9112 Messages, Methods and Security | Safeguard Blog
passages: SS

HTTP/1.1 is the text based version of the Hypertext Transfer Protocol: a client sends a request line, header fields and an optional body over a TCP connection, and the server answers with a status line, header fields and a body.
Since June 2022 it has been defined by RFC 9112 (the HTTP/1.1 message syntax), RFC 9110 (the semantics every HTTP version shares) and RFC 9111 (caching), which together replaced RFC 7230 to RFC 7235.
The protocol is old, simple and still everywhere.
## Key takeaways

* HTTP/1.1 is now specified across three documents published in June 2022: RFC 9110 "HTTP Semantics" (STD 97), RFC 9111 "HTTP Caching" (STD 98) and RFC 9112 "HTTP/1.1" (STD 99). RFC 9110 obsoletes RFC 2818 and RFC 7230 to 7235 (except 7234), RFC 9111 obsoletes RFC 7234, and RFC 9112 obsoletes the message syntax parts of RFC 7230.

* A message is a start line, zero or more field lines, an empty line and an optional body. The default port is TCP 80 for `http` URIs and TCP 443 for `https` URIs, per RFC 9110 sections 4.2.1 and 4.2.2.
| RFC 9111 | HTTP Caching | 98 | June 2022 | RFC 7234 |
| RFC 9112 | HTTP/1.1 | 99 | June 2022 | Portions of RFC 7230 |
| RFC 9113 | HTTP/2 | n/a | June 2022 | (HTTP/2 framing, referenced by RFC 9110) |
| RFC 9114 | HTTP/3 | n/a | June 2022 | (HTTP/3 over QUIC, referenced by RFC 9110) |

RFC 9110 now holds everything that applies to every HTTP version: methods, status codes, header field semantics, content negotiation, conditional requests, range requests, authentication, and the `http` and `https` schemes.

HTTP-message = start-line CRLF *( field-line CRLF ) CRLF [ message-body ] start-line = request-line / status-line request-line = method SP request-target SP HTTP-version status-line = HTTP-version SP status-code SP [ reason-phrase ] field-line = field-name ":" OWS field-value OWS
RFC 9110 section 9 defines eight methods and classifies each as safe (read only in intent) and idempotent (repeating it has the same intended effect as sending it once):
| Method | Purpose | Safe | Idempotent |
These properties are not trivia.
RFC 9110 explains that idempotent requests "can be repeated automatically if a communication failure occurs", and that a proxy "MUST NOT automatically retry non-idempotent requests".

TRACE reflects the received request back to the client, and RFC 9110 warns that a client must not put sensitive data in a TRACE request and that the final recipient should strip fields likely to carry it.
### Persistent connections
HTTP/1.0 opened a new TCP connection for every request unless both sides used the nonstandard `Keep-Alive` mechanism.
HTTP/1.1 reversed the default.
Responses carry no identifier tying them to requests; order is the only link.
Clients should not pipeline after a non idempotent method until its final response arrives.
That ordering rule is why HTTP/1.1 suffers from head of line blocking: one slow response holds up every response behind it.
| RFC 7230 to RFC 7235 | June 2014 | HTTP/1.1 split into six documents (message syntax, semantics, conditional requests, range requests, caching, authentication) |
| RFC 9110, 9111, 9112 | June 2022 | Version independent semantics separated from HTTP/1.1 syntax; stricter parsing to resist smuggling |
| HTTP/2, RFC 9113 | June 2022 | A multiplexed session layer with field compression over TLS and TCP, sharing RFC 9110 semantics |
| HTTP/3, RFC 9114 | June 2022 | HTTP over QUIC, a secure multiplexed transport over UDP |
RFC 9110 says HTTP/1.1 "was introduced in 1995" before its 1997 publication.
The design allows this because of several historical tolerances:

* **Two length signals.** Content-Length and Transfer-Encoding can both appear. RFC 9112 explains that early implementations sent both, a chunked body plus an estimated length "for use by progress bars", which is why the standard made Transfer-Encoding override Content-Length rather than forbidding the combination. Any hop that does not follow that rule exactly, or that only speaks HTTP/1.0, can disagree with the others.

* **Lenient whitespace and line endings.** RFC 9112 lets recipients treat a bare LF as a line ending and lets them parse request lines on any whitespace. It immediately warns that "lenient parsing can result in request smuggling security vulnerabilities if there are multiple recipients of the message and each has its own unique interpretation of robustness".
RFC 9110 section 17.5 notes that because HTTP uses "mostly textual, character-delimited fields", parsers are often vulnerable to "very long (or very slow) streams of data".

The standard sets minimum sizes that implementations should support but leaves the maximums to operators, and warns that failing to limit method names, field names, numeric values and chunk lengths "can result in arbitrary code execution due to buffer or arithmetic overflows".
That is why server limits on header size, header count, body size and read timeouts are security settings, not just tuning.
Then confirm what nginx actually loaded.

pages.title: What Are Safe and Idempotent HTTP Methods? · JobCannon
passages: # What Are Safe and Idempotent HTTP Methods?
## Short Answer

**A safe HTTP method is intended only for fetching information, not for causing changes on the server. An idempotent method has the same intended effect whether a request is sent once or many times. The difference matters because a failed idempotent request can be retried automatically, whereas retrying one that creates something may do it twice.**
## Full Answer
Both ideas come from RFC 9110, HTTP Semantics (June 2022), which defines them in sections 9.2.1 and 9.2.2.
### Safe
the RFC says a request method is safe if it is intended only for fetching information and not for causing changes on the origin server.
It lists GET, HEAD, OPTIONS and TRACE as the safe methods it defines.
Safe describes what the client is asking for, not that the server does nothing else, so a server may still write a log entry.
### Idempotent
a request method is idempotent if the intended effect of a request is the same whether it is executed once or multiple times.
The RFC states that every safe method is also idempotent, and it names two more methods that are idempotent although they are not safe.
Idempotence concerns the effect on the server, not the response, so a repeated request may get a different status code back.
### Why it matters
the RFC allows clients to retry idempotent requests automatically after a connection failure, and it lets intermediaries do the same after a failure or timeout.
A method that is not idempotent, such as one that creates a new order, has no such guarantee, so a blind retry after a timeout can repeat the action.
API designers add their own protection against duplicates for those requests, and clients should not retry them without it.
### Habit to build
before choosing a method, ask what a repeat would do.
If a repeat would cause harm, the design needs another safeguard.
### Find Out for Yourself
Take the REST API Testfree — see your result with strengths, blind spots.
## Related Questions
Is every idempotent method safe?▼
No.
Every safe method is idempotent, but the reverse is not true.
RFC 9110 names some methods that are idempotent because repeating them leaves the same result, even though they do change the server.
Why should a GET request never change data?▼
Because GET is defined as safe.
Clients, caches and other software are entitled to treat it as read-only, so a GET that changes data can be triggered by accident.
## More on Just for Fun
[What Is a Cybersecurity Awareness Test?

A cybersecurity awareness test is a short multiple-choice check of the everyday habits that keep an employer safe, such as spotting a phishing email, protecting a login, handling information with care and reporting a mistake early.
It asks what a sensible employee would do in a workplace situation, not how computer systems work.](/answers/what-is-a-cybersecurity-awareness-test)[How Can You Tell If an Email Is Phishing?

Look for pressure and for a request you did not expect: urgent or emotional language, a request for personal or financial information, a shortened link, or an email address or link that is not quite right.

The safest habit is not to trust how a message looks but to check it another way, using contact details you look up yourself.](/answers/how-can-you-tell-if-an-email-is-phishing)[What Makes a Good Password for Work?
A good work password is long, hard to guess and not used anywhere else.

UK and US government guidance suggests combining three random words, or using a password manager to create and store long random passwords, and avoiding dates, names and common passwords.](/answers/what-makes-a-good-password-for-work)[What Is Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA)?
Multi-factor authentication (MFA) means proving who you are with more than a password, for example a password plus a code from an app or a fingerprint.
If someone learns your password, they still need the second factor to get in.](/answers/what-is-multi-factor-authentication)[What Does a Work VPN Do, and What Does It Not Do?
A work VPN creates an encrypted connection between your device and your organisation, so that data in transit across a network you do not control, such as public Wi-Fi, is protected.

It only protects the traffic that is sent through it, and it does not make a phishing email or a risky download safe.](/answers/what-does-a-work-vpn-do)[What Should You Do If You Make a Security Mistake at Work?
Tell your employer’s IT or security contact straight away, even if you are not sure it matters, and do not hide it or try to fix it quietly.

The sooner the right people know, the sooner they can limit the harm, and UK national guidance says staff should feel supported to come forward even when they have clicked.](/answers/what-to-do-after-a-security-mistake-at-work)

pages.title: RFC 9110 Explained: Safe & Idempotent HTTP Methods
passages: # RFC 9110 Explained: Safe & Idempotent HTTP Methods
A practical guide to safe, idempotent, and cacheable HTTP methods, with examples and links to the official RFC 9110 sections.
[RFC 9110](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110) is the IETF standard that defines HTTP semantics.
The IETF published it in June 2022 as Internet Standard STD 97.
Roy Fielding, Mark Nottingham, and Julian Reschke edited it.
Roy Fielding also wrote the 2000 dissertation that defined REST.
RFC 9110 defines what HTTP messages mean, and not how a particular version transmits them.
The same semantics apply to HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, and HTTP/3.
A safe method does not request a state change.
An idempotent method has the same intended effect when a client repeats an identical request.
For REST API work, three parts of RFC 9110 matter most.
Section 9.2 classifies methods as safe, idempotent, or cacheable.
Section 9.3 defines each method.
## What Is a Target Resource in RFC 9110?
A resource is the thing an HTTP request addresses.
A target URI identifies that resource.
A representation describes its state in a format such as JSON.
An HTTP resource does not require a database row.
A response body carries a representation of the resource.
One resource can have different representations.

[Section 3.1](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110#section-3.1) defines resources. [Section 3.2](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110#section-3.2) explains representations. [Section 7.1](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110#section-7.1) explains how a request identifies its target URI.
GET /books/42 HTTP/1.1 Host: api.example.com Accept: application/json HTTP/1.1 200 OK Content-Type: application/json { "id": 42, "title": "HTTP in Practice" }
This table records what RFC 9110 states for each method it defines.
PATCH is included for comparison, but a separate standard defines it.
| Method | Safe | Idempotent | Cacheable | Section |
\*RFC 5789 defines PATCH, not RFC 9110.
A server can make PATCH idempotent by design, but the standard does not require it.
## Safe Methods (Section 9.2.1)
A method is safe when its defined semantics are read-only.
The client does not request a state change on the origin server, and does not expect one.
Note the limit of the guarantee.
A safe method can still produce a side effect, such as a log entry or an analytics event.
The rule constrains what the client asks for, not what the server records.
A method is idempotent when the intended effect of two or more identical requests is the same as the effect of one request.
[Section 9.2.2](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110#section-9.2.2) states that **PUT**, **DELETE**, and the safe request methods are idempotent.
The safe methods are GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, and TRACE.

# Idempotent: the resource holds the same value after one request or ten PUT /users/123 { "name": "Ada", "email": "ada@example.com" } # Idempotent: after the first request the resource is gone and stays gone DELETE /users/123 # NOT idempotent: each request creates another user POST /users { "name": "Ada", "email": "ada@example.com" }
Idempotency is what makes a retry safe.
If a network failure hides the response to a PUT or a DELETE, the client can send the request again without risk.
A retried POST creates a duplicate, so POST needs an [idempotency key](/idempotency) to become safe to retry.
As with safe methods, the guarantee covers the intended effect only.
A server can log each request separately or keep a revision history for every idempotent request.
## Methods and Caching (Section 9.2.3)
* **PUT, DELETE, CONNECT, OPTIONS, TRACE** — responses are not cacheable
A cached POST response can satisfy a later GET or HEAD request for the same URI.
In practice almost no API relies on this, and most caches never store a POST response.
| 9.3.6 | CONNECT | Establish a tunnel to the origin server |
| 9.3.7 | OPTIONS | Request the communication options for a resource |
| 9.3.8 | TRACE | Request a loop-back of the request message |
Our [HTTP methods guide](/http-methods) covers each of these with request and response examples.
The [OPTIONS deep dive](/http-methods-options) covers CORS preflight in detail.
This causes a common error.
Developers look for PATCH in Section 9.3, do not find it, and conclude that PATCH is non-standard.
PATCH is standard.
A server can design an idempotent PATCH.
Our [PATCH deep dive](/http-methods-patch) shows how, and covers JSON Patch and JSON Merge Patch.
## What RFC 9110 Replaced
The change was structural rather than semantic.
The IETF split HTTP into a semantics document (RFC 9110) and separate documents per version.
| 9.2 | Common method properties | [Idempotency](/idempotency) |
| 9.3 | Method definitions | [HTTP methods](/http-methods) |
| 10 | Message context header fields | [HTTP headers](/http-headers) |
### Which HTTP methods are idempotent in RFC 9110?
Section 9.2.2 states that PUT, DELETE, and the safe request methods are idempotent.
The safe methods are GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, and TRACE.
POST and CONNECT are not idempotent.
### Which HTTP methods are safe in RFC 9110?
Section 9.2.1 defines GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, and TRACE as safe.
A safe method is read-only in its defined semantics.
Every safe method is also idempotent.
### Which HTTP methods are cacheable in RFC 9110?
No.
RFC 5789 defines PATCH separately.
### What is the difference between safe and idempotent?
A safe method does not change server state at all.
An idempotent method can change state, but two or more identical requests have the same effect as one.
Every safe method is idempotent.
PUT and DELETE are idempotent but not safe.
Cite RFC 9110.
It obsoleted RFC 7231 in June 2022.
The semantics did not change, but RFC 7231 is no longer the current reference.
[### 📘 HTTP Methods
Every method with request and response examples.](/http-methods) [### 🔁 Idempotency
Idempotency keys and safe retries for POST.](/idempotency) [### 🔢 Status Codes
The status codes defined in Section 15.](/status-codes) [### 🩹 PATCH Deep Dive
The method RFC 9110 does not define.](/http-methods-patch)

passages: * J. Reschke, Ed.
Internet Standard
## [Copyright Notice](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#name-copyright-notice)
Copyright (c) 2022 IETF Trust and the persons identified as the document authors.
All rights reserved.[¶](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#section-boilerplate.2-1)

The client examines received responses to see if its intentions were carried out, determining what to do next based on the status codes and content received.[¶](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#section-1.3-2)

HTTP semantics include the intentions defined by each request method ([Section 9](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#methods)), extensions to those semantics that might be described in request header fields, status codes that describe the response ([Section 15](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#status.codes)), and other control data and resource metadata that might be given in response fields.[¶](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#section-1.3-3)

Semantics also include representation metadata that describe how content is intended to be interpreted by a recipient, request header fields that might influence content selection, and the various selection algorithms that are collectively referred to as "content negotiation" ([Section 12](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#content.negotiation)).[¶](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#section-1.3-4)

This specification uses the Augmented Backus-Naur Form (ABNF) notation of [[RFC5234](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#RFC5234)], extended with the notation for case-sensitivity in strings defined in [[RFC7405](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#RFC7405)].[¶](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#section-2.1-1)

It also uses a list extension, defined in [Section 5.6.1](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#abnf.extension), that allows for compact definition of comma-separated lists using a "#" operator (similar to how the "*" operator indicates repetition). [Appendix A](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#collected.abnf) shows the collected grammar with all list operators expanded to standard ABNF notation.[¶](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#section-2.1-2)
As a convention, ABNF rule names prefixed with "obs-" denote obsolete grammar rules that appear for historical reasons.[¶](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#section-2.1-3)

For example, a Web browser might wish to transparently recover from a response where the [Location](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#field.location) header field doesn't parse according to the ABNF, whereas a systems control client might consider any form of error recovery to be dangerous.[¶](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#section-2.4-2)

Some requests can be automatically retried by a client in the event of an underlying connection failure, as described in [Section 9.2.2](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#idempotent.methods).[¶](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#section-2.4-3)
### [2.5.](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#section-2.5)[Protocol Version](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#name-protocol-version)
## [3.](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#section-3)[Terminology and Core Concepts](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#name-terminology-and-core-concep)
HTTP was created for the World Wide Web (WWW) architecture and has evolved over time to support the scalability needs of a worldwide hypertext system.
Much of that architecture is reflected in the terminology used to define HTTP.[¶](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#section-3-1)
The target of an HTTP request is called a "resource".

Most resources are identified by a Uniform Resource Identifier (URI), as described in [Section 4](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#uri).[¶](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#section-3.1-1)
A resource cannot treat a request in a manner inconsistent with the semantics of the method of the request.

For example, though the URI of a resource might imply semantics that are not safe, a client can expect the resource to avoid actions that are unsafe when processing a request with a safe method (see [Section 9.2.1](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#safe.methods)).[¶](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#section-3.1-2)

HTTP relies upon the Uniform Resource Identifier (URI) standard [[URI](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#URI)] to indicate the target resource ([Section 7.1](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#target.resource)) and relationships between resources.[¶](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#section-3.1-3)
As a result, a server MUST NOT assume that two requests on the same connection are from the same user agent unless the connection is secured and specific to that agent.

Some non-standard HTTP extensions (e.g., [[RFC4559](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#RFC4559)]) have been known to violate this requirement, resulting in security and interoperability problems.[¶](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#section-3.3-5)
### [3.4.](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#section-3.4)[Messages](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#name-messages)
request >

Field values containing CR, LF, or NUL characters are invalid and dangerous, due to the varying ways that implementations might parse and interpret those characters; a recipient of CR, LF, or NUL within a field value MUST either reject the message or replace each of those characters with SP before further processing or forwarding of that message.

Field values containing other CTL characters are also invalid; however, recipients MAY retain such characters for the sake of robustness when they appear within a safe context (e.g., an application-specific quoted string that will not be processed by any downstream HTTP parser).[¶](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#section-5.5-5)
Fields that only anticipate a single member as the field value are referred to as "singleton fields".[¶](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#section-5.5-6)

pages.title: What Is Idempotency? HTTP Methods and Keys - LoadFocus
passages: # What is Idempotency? HTTP Methods, Idempotency Keys, Examples
## Idempotency means repeating an operation leaves the same state as doing it once. See which HTTP methods qualify and how keys make POST safe to retry.
## What is idempotency?
An operation is idempotent if doing it several times leaves the system in the same state as doing it once.
In HTTP, that means a client can repeat a request after a timeout or a dropped connection without causing a second charge, order or email.
GET, PUT and DELETE are idempotent by definition.
POST is not.
Idempotent design makes retries safe.
## Idempotency in HTTP methods
[RFC 9110](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110#section-9.2.2) (which replaced RFC 7231) says PUT, DELETE and all safe methods are idempotent:
| Method | Idempotent? | Why |
| GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, TRACE | Yes | Safe methods: they read, they do not change state |
| PUT | Yes | Replaces the resource with the same representation every time |
| DELETE | Yes | The first call removes the resource, later calls find nothing left to remove |
| POST | No | Typically creates a new resource or triggers an action on every call |
| PATCH | Not guaranteed | Depends on the patch: setting a value is idempotent, incrementing is not |
Idempotent does not mean "returns the same response".
The property describes the intended effect on the server, not the response.
RFC 5789 notes that a PATCH request can be issued in a way that makes it idempotent.
## Examples
## Why idempotency matters
* **Timeouts and dropped connections.** The client cannot tell whether the server processed the request before the connection failed. With an idempotent operation it can simply retry.

* **Automatic retries.** RFC 9110 lets clients retry idempotent requests automatically after a connection failure, and says a proxy must not automatically retry a non-idempotent one. SDKs and service meshes follow similar rules.
## Idempotency keys

For operations that are not naturally idempotent, such as creating an order or charging a card, the common pattern is an **idempotency key**: a unique value the client generates for one logical operation and sends with every attempt of it.
POST /charges HTTP/1.1 Idempotency-Key: 8e0a4e6b-1b8e-4e3a-b9f7-5e1d3f9c4b8a Content-Type: application/json {"amount": 5000, "currency": "usd"}
A repeat with the same key returns the stored result instead of running the operation again.

Stripe is the best-known example and documents the details: the `Idempotency-Key` header, keys of up to 255 characters, V4 UUIDs suggested, and for API v1 the status code and body of the first request saved and replayed, including 500 errors.
Keys can be pruned after at least 24 hours, and reusing a key with different parameters returns an error.
It is still an Internet-Draft, not an RFC.
It describes a 409 response when a retry arrives while the original request is still running, and a 422 when a key is reused with a different payload.
### Implementing keys on the server
1. Read the key from the request and store it with a fingerprint of the request body.
2. Look the key up. If a finished result exists and the fingerprint matches, return it without side effects.
3. If the fingerprint differs, reject the request (422 in the draft).
* **New key per retry.** The key belongs to the operation, not the attempt. If each retry generates a fresh key, nothing is deduplicated.
* **Forgetting side effects outside the database.** An "idempotent" endpoint that sends an email on every call is not idempotent.
* **No expiry.** Keeping every key forever grows storage without limit. Pick a window that covers your clients' retries.
* **Race conditions.** Two simultaneous requests with one key can both run unless you lock or use a unique constraint.
* **Mixing up safe and idempotent.** Safe means no state change (GET). PUT and DELETE are idempotent but not safe.
## Idempotency in load testing and monitoring

* **Non-idempotent endpoints pile up data.** A POST test creates records on every iteration, so plan cleanup or use a test environment. At a 5-minute interval, a monitoring check that posts runs 288 times a day, so prefer a read-only check or a dedicated test endpoint.
* **Generate a unique key per virtual user and iteration.** If every virtual user reuses one key, they all get the stored first response and your test only loaded the first request.
* **Test the mechanism itself.** Send the same request twice, and concurrently, and assert that the responses match and only one record exists. See [API testing](/glossary/what-is-api-testing).
### Is GET always idempotent?
By definition, yes: GET is a safe method and should not change state.
Some APIs misuse GET for actions such as tracking or unsubscribing, which breaks that rule and lets prefetching and retries trigger the action.
### What is the difference between idempotent and safe?
Safe means the request is not meant to change server state (GET, HEAD, OPTIONS).
Idempotent means repeating it has the same intended effect as sending it once.
PUT and DELETE are idempotent but not safe.
### How do I make a POST request idempotent?
Send an idempotency key, a unique value for the operation that you reuse on every retry.
The server stores the first result under that key and returns it for repeats.
Yes.

GraphQL queries read data, while mutations need their own protection, for example a key passed in the input. gRPC lets a method be marked as idempotent in its definition, which tells clients when a retry is safe.
## Related terms
